title: Partitioning with Concrete Models
objective: Specify and partition a whole into equal parts, identifying and counting unit fractions using concrete models.

problems.text: A beaker is considered full when the liquid reaches the fill line shown near the top. Estimate the amount of water in the beaker by shading the drawing as indicated.
Juanita cut her string cheese into equal pieces as shown in the rectangles below. In the blanks below, name the fraction of the string cheese represented by the shaded part.
problems.note: Multiple rectangles with varying partitions and shading - student names each fraction

problems.text: Draw a small rectangle. Estimate to split it into 2 equal parts. How many lines did you draw to make 2 equal parts? What is the name of each fractional unit?
Draw another small rectangle. Estimate to split it into 3 equal parts. How many lines did you draw to make 3 equal parts? What is the name of each fractional unit?
Draw another small rectangle. Estimate to split it into 4 equal parts. How many lines did you draw to make 4 equal parts? What is the name of each fractional unit?
Each rectangle represents 1 sheet of paper. Estimate to show how you would cut the paper into fractional units as indicated below.

followup.question: What do you notice? How many lines do you think you would draw to make a rectangle with 20 equal parts?
followup.pattern: Number of lines = number of parts - 1

problems.text: Rochelle has a strip of wood 12 inches long. She cuts it into pieces that are each 6 inches in length. What fraction of the wood is one piece? Draw a picture to show the piece of wood and how Rochelle cut it.

answer.reasoning: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 pieces, so each piece is 1 of 2 equal parts
